title: I asked Gemini to order dinner, but Google's keeping that feature for itself
excerpt: Android fragmentation found a new place to show up
content_html:
Published Sep 16, 2026, 11:15 AM EDT

Ali has spent more than a decade covering consumer technology, with a knack for looking beyond the specs, tinkering with software, and uncovering the bigger stories behind Android, Google, Apple, and everyday devices.

I asked Gemini to order me a chicken burger. A simple request, exactly the kind of thing that agentic AI is supposed to exist for.

Gemini's response was kind of rude, or maybe I was just hungry. It told me it can't place orders directly for me and that I would have to use a food delivery app like Foodpanda, or the delivery app of my choice.

No attempt, no app opened, just the same uneven feature rollout Android's always been known for. Gemini pointed me to the manual app grid I was trying to avoid.

I tried naming the app next, requesting it order me a chicken burger from Foodpanda. Everything was installed and set up on my phone.

I got the same fallback message, word for word.

What actually happened, twice

The same flat refusal, no matter how I asked

Neither prompt got so much as an attempt. Gemini didn't launch Foodpanda, didn't ask which restaurant, and didn't acknowledge that the app existed on my phone.

It just repeated the same generic line each time I tried.

That's the kind of response that reads the same when the feature doesn't exist, isn't available to you, or it didn't understand the request.

I wondered if I was using the right words or if the request wasn't understandable.

The real reason has nothing to do with confusion

My phone, and probably yours, isn't invited

Gemini's food and ride ordering feature is real. There isn't a problem with the feature. I've seen it work flawlessly online, in videos and demos from people using it on compatible phones, just not on mine.

It launched earlier this year in beta, and it works for the people it was built for, just not on hardware like mine.

Google's support documentation limits it to the Pixel 10, Pixel 10 Pro, Pixel 10 Pro XL, and the Samsung Galaxy S26 series, Galaxy Z Flip 8, and Z Fold 8. That's a narrow slate for a company that ships Android on more phone models than any other OS in the world.

It's also restricted to users 18 and up, in the US or Korea only, with no timeline given for wider availability.

My Pixel 8 is two generations behind the cutoff, and the Foodpanda app isn't on the confirmed list of supported apps, which leans towards names like DoorDash, Uber Eats, and Grubhub.

I was locked out twice, on the device and on the app, and Gemini never gave me a reason each time.

This isn't really a story about my phone

Almost the entire Android install base is on the outside of this

Android runs on billions of active devices, spread across dozens of manufacturers and price points.

This feature only works on two device families, in exactly two countries. Everyone else, including me, is stuck watching keynote demos of a feature that doesn't function.

That is not a small footnote. That's most of Google's audience being unable to use a feature it's actively marketing as the future of the operating system, in keynote after keynote.

Google has been trying to smooth out Android's old update fragmentation, only to open a new one shaped entirely around who gets the new AI features first.

This is the same pattern playing out again, just showing up as a dinner order instead of a settings menu buried three taps deep.

Gemini's silence is the actual design problem

A refusal that looks identical to confusion

If Gemini had said this feature isn't available in my region or that my device isn't supported, it would have been a reasonable answer.

Instead, it gave me the same generic non-answer a confused assistant would give.

That distinction holds importance. One response tells you to stop wasting your time on something that will never work, and the other just makes the AI look broken.

A little honesty from Gemini would have saved me two identical attempts and a few minutes of assuming I had done something wrong.

Most Android owners are going to hit the same wall

And they won't know why either

I'm not the only one running into a version of this.

Plenty of Android owners have discovered that a shiny new feature they heard about wasn't reaching their phone.

Google, on the flip side, has never explained it up front for any device.

Ask Gemini to order your dinner, and odds are you'll get the same refusal I did, regardless of which app you're using. Google gets to claim the feature exists the moment it ships to anyone, even if that's only 1% of the Android user base.

It's not you, and it's not even about Foodpanda. It's about a feature built for a small slice of Android phones, marketed like it's for all of them.
